title: Area Theorems for Quantum Error Correction
authors: Avijit Mandal, Mert Gökduman, Henry D. Pfister
abstract: The extrinsic information transfer (EXIT) and generalized EXIT (GEXIT) area theorems provide fundamental conservation laws that connect the rate of classical codes to the performance of maximum-a-posteriori decoding on binary memoryless channels. In this work, we generalize these area theorems to quantum error correction. We first develop a coset-entropy formalism for nested linear codes, where the message specifies a coset and encoder randomization selects a codeword within that coset. The area under the resulting coset (G)EXIT function equals the normalized dimension of the quotient. For stabilizer codes, the measured syndrome restricts the Pauli error but does not always determine its logical effect, and the remaining uncertainty is an entropy over logical correction classes. We show that this entropy equals a classical coset entropy associated with the stabilizer group and the Pauli operators that commute with it. The resulting quantum GEXIT function has area equal to the number of encoded qubits per channel use for any stabilizer code, and this applies to the depolarizing channel through its joint four-valued Pauli-error distribution. For CSS codes on the quantum erasure channel and under independent bit- and phase-flip noise, the logical correction problem separates into two binary coset-decoding problems. On the quantum erasure channel, the duality between the stabilizer group and the Pauli operators that commute with it gives a folding identity at complementary erasure probabilities. Using this and the area theorem, we derive an upper bound on the rate of code families with vanishing logical error probability that matches the capacity of the quantum erasure channel. For the depolarizing channel, we also derive a rate-dependent converse, using a connection between correction-class entropy and coherent information to establish an inequality involving the complementary channel.
summary: This work extends classical area theorems to the quantum domain to establish fundamental rate constraints for quantum error correction. By developing a coset-entropy formalism, the authors show that the area under the quantum GEXIT function quantifies the code's performance relative to the channel capacity. This provides powerful, mathematically rigorous tools for designing and analyzing quantum codes.
main_problem: The paper generalizes classical area theorems, originally for classical error correction, to derive fundamental rate constraints for quantum error correction codes.
main_result: The area under the quantum GEXIT function equals the number of encoded qubits per channel use for stabilizer codes, and the area theorem yields capacity-matching upper bounds for specific quantum channels.
method: The authors develop a coset-entropy formalism and apply the fundamental theorem of calculus to relate the integral of normalized entropy functions (GEXIT) to the dimension of the code quotient.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on quantum error correction, specifically examining stabilizer codes and CSS codes under various noise models, including the quantum erasure channel, depolarizing channel, and independent bit- and phase-flip noise.
key_observables: The area under the GEXIT function, correction-class entropy, and the rate $k/n$ are key observables used to derive bounds.
important_parameters: Erasure probability ($\epsilon$), crossover/flip probability ($p$), and the code rate ($k/n$) are critical parameters analyzed across different noise regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the equivalence between syndrome decoding and classical coset decoding, and the assumption of memorylessness for the channels considered.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the entropy functions ($\gamma_Q(\epsilon)$) for the quantum erasure channel and show the decomposition of these functions for planar surface codes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the coset-entropy formalism, then deriving the classical area theorems, extending these theorems to stabilizer codes for specific channels, and finally deriving rate-dependent converse bounds.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework connecting information-theoretic concepts (entropy, area theorems) to physical constraints (channel capacity) provides powerful tools for analyzing the limits of quantum computation.
